claims.text: The starting high-entropy alloy is homogeneously disordered, with a random distribution of constituent elements.
The starting alloy shows no superconductivity or only weak superconducting signatures at low temperature.
Controlled thermal annealing can promote short-range compositional order without causing bulk phase separation.
Annealing induces clustering or ordering of selected constituent elements.
Annealing-induced local compositional order decreases lattice disorder.
Decreased lattice disorder reduces electron scattering.
Decreased lattice disorder enhances or softens specific phonon modes.
Softer phonon modes more effectively mediate electron pairing.
Improved electron-phonon-mediated Cooper pairing facilitates the emergence of superconductivity in the alloy.
Annealed samples will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will show sharper resistive superconducting transitions than as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will show sharper magnetic-susceptibility transitions than as-cast samples.
The untreated alloy has higher residual resistivity than the proposed annealed state.
The proposed mechanism applies only where moderate annealing increases local order without inducing phase separation.
Excessive annealing can cause phase segregation and prevent the proposed superconductivity enhancement.
The effect may fail when intrinsic disorder is too severe to be remedied by annealing.

contradictions.description: Testing only below the expected superconducting transition region is inconsistent with determining and comparing the transition temperature from temperature-dependent resistivity and susceptibility; the measurement sweep must span the transition region.

The falsification rule requires that no increase in local ordering be detected. That condition means the intended mediator was not successfully produced, so failure to improve superconductivity would not decisively contradict the claim that increased ordering causes the improvement.
